summary.text: Deleting zero digits preserves decimal digit sum, while every positive multiple of \(10^k-1\) has digit sum at least \(9k\); hence every reachable value at step \(10^k-1\) is at least \(10^{k-1}\). Thus \(a(10^k-1)\ge 10^{k-1}\) for all \(k\ge1\), which grows without bound.

full_proof.text:
Let \(Z(x)\) denote the natural number obtained from the usual decimal representation of \(x\) by deleting every digit equal to \(0\). (Set \(Z(0)=0\), although zero will not occur along any path considered below.) Define the finite sets of reachable values recursively by
\[
R_0=\{1\},
\qquad
R_{n+1}=\bigcup_{u\in R_n}\{(n+1)u,\;Z((n+1)u)\}.
\]
Thus \(R_n\) is exactly the set of possible values at time \(n\) when, after each multiplication, one may either retain the product or delete all of its zero digits. The sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=\min R_n.
\]
Each \(R_n\) is finite and nonempty: this is immediate by induction, since from any member of \(R_n\) one can at least retain the product at the next step.

We will prove the much stronger lower bounds
\[
\boxed{\ a(10^k-1)\ge 10^{k-1}\ }
\qquad(k\ge 1).
\]
Since the right-hand side tends to infinity, these bounds disprove boundedness.

Define the decimal digit sum of a natural number \(x\) by
\[
s(x)=\text{the sum of the decimal digits of }x.
\]
In particular, \(s(0)=0\). Deleting zero digits does not affect a digit sum, so
\[
s(Z(x))=s(x)                                                    \tag{1}
\]
for every \(x\). Also, if \(x>0\), then \(s(x)\ge 1\), since the leading digit of a positive integer is nonzero. Consequently \(Z(x)>0\) whenever \(x>0\).

It follows by induction that every reachable value is positive. Indeed, the only value in \(R_0\) is \(1\). If \(u\in R_n\) is positive, then \((n+1)u>0\), and both possible successors, namely \((n+1)u\) and \(Z((n+1)u)\), are positive. We will use this positivity at the special final step \(n=10^k-1\).

We first establish the elementary decimal facts needed for the main argument.

**Digit-sum subadditivity.** For all natural numbers \(x,y\),
\[
s(x+y)\le s(x)+s(y).                                           \tag{2}
\]
Here is a proof that explicitly accounts for carries. We use strong induction on \(N=x+y\). The assertion is immediate if \(x=0\) or \(y=0\). Suppose both are positive. Write
\[
x=10x_1+x_0,\qquad y=10y_1+y_0,
\]
where \(0\le x_0,y_0\le 9\). Let
\[
c=\left\lfloor\frac{x_0+y_0}{10}\right\rfloor.
\]
Because \(x_0+y_0\le18\), the carry \(c\) is either \(0\) or \(1\). If \(N=10N_1+N_0\), then decimal addition gives
\[
N_1=x_1+y_1+c,
\qquad
N_0+c\le x_0+y_0.                                               \tag{3}
\]
In fact the second relation is an equality when \(c=0\), while when \(c=1\) one has \(N_0+10=x_0+y_0\), and hence certainly the displayed inequality.

Both \(N_1\) and \(y_1+c\) are strictly smaller than \(N\) in the nontrivial case, so strong induction may be applied first to
\(N_1=x_1+(y_1+c)\), and then to \(y_1+c=y_1+c\). This yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
s(N_1)&\le s(x_1)+s(y_1+c),\\
s(y_1+c)&\le s(y_1)+s(c).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(c\in\{0,1\}\), we have \(s(c)=c\). Using the decimal recurrences
\[
s(N)=N_0+s(N_1),\quad s(x)=x_0+s(x_1),\quad s(y)=y_0+s(y_1),
\]
and (3), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
s(N)
&=N_0+s(N_1)\\
&\le N_0+s(x_1)+s(y_1+c)\\
&\le N_0+s(x_1)+s(y_1)+c\\
&\le x_0+y_0+s(x_1)+s(y_1)\\
&=s(x)+s(y).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (2).

We will also use the following block decomposition property. If \(q>0\) and \(0\le r<10^k\), then
\[
s(10^kq+r)=s(q)+s(r).                                          \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, multiplication of \(q\) by \(10^k\) appends \(k\) zero positions. Since \(r<10^k\), adding \(r\) fills only those final \(k\) positions and causes no carry into the digits of \(q\). If the decimal representation of \(r\) has fewer than \(k\) digits, it is padded on the left with zeros, which do not affect its digit sum. Thus the digits of \(10^kq+r\) consist of the digits of \(q\), followed by a block of \(k\) digits representing \(r\), and (4) follows.

For later comparison between digit sum and size, note that every decimal digit is at most \(9\). Therefore an integer having at most \(j\) decimal digits has digit sum at most \(9j\). In particular,
\[
x<10^j\quad\Longrightarrow\quad s(x)\le 9j.                   \tag{5}
\]
This includes \(x=0\); for positive \(x\), it is simply the familiar fact that numbers below \(10^j\) have at most \(j\) digits.

The central fact is the following.

**Lemma.** If \(k\ge1\), then every positive multiple \(M\) of
\[
m=10^k-1
\]
satisfies
\[
s(M)\ge 9k.                                                    \tag{6}
\]

To prove the lemma, fix \(k\ge1\) and use strong induction on the positive multiple \(M\).

First suppose
\[
M<10^k=m+1.
\]
Write \(M=mt\). Since \(M>0\), we have \(t\ge1\). If \(t\ge2\), then
\[
M=mt\ge2m=2(10^k-1)\ge10^k,
\]
because \(10^k\ge10\). This contradicts \(M<10^k\). Hence \(t=1\), so
\[
M=m=10^k-1.
\]
Its decimal representation consists of exactly \(k\) digits, all equal to \(9\). Thus
\[
s(M)=9k,
\]
and (6) holds in this case.

Now suppose
\[
M\ge10^k.
\]
Divide \(M\) by \(10^k\), writing
\[
M=10^kq+r,
\qquad q\ge1,
\qquad 0\le r<10^k.                                             \tag{7}
\]
Since \(10^k=m+1\), equation (7) can be rewritten as
\[
M=(m+1)q+r=mq+(q+r).                                             \tag{8}
\]
By assumption \(m\mid M\), and of course \(m\mid mq\). Subtracting the latter multiple from (8) shows that
\[
m\mid(q+r).                                                     \tag{9}
\]
Moreover, \(q+r>0\) because \(q\ge1\), and
\[
q+r<M
\]
because (8) expresses \(M\) as \(q+r\) plus the strictly positive quantity \(mq\). Thus \(q+r\) is a smaller positive multiple of \(m\). The strong induction hypothesis applied to it gives
\[
s(q+r)\ge9k.                                                    \tag{10}
\]
On the other hand, digit-sum subadditivity gives
\[
s(q+r)\le s(q)+s(r),                                           \tag{11}
\]
while the block decomposition (4), applied to (7), gives
\[
s(M)=s(q)+s(r).                                                 \tag{12}
\]
Combining (10), (11), and (12), we conclude
\[
s(M)=s(q)+s(r)\ge s(q+r)\ge9k.
\]
This completes both cases of the strong induction and proves the lemma.

The lemma immediately gives a lower bound on the numerical size of any positive multiple of \(10^k-1\), even after its zero digits have been removed. More precisely, if \(k\ge1\) and a number \(x\) satisfies
\[
s(x)\ge9k,
\]
then
\[
x\ge10^{k-1}.                                                   \tag{13}
\]
For if instead \(x<10^{k-1}\), then (5), with \(j=k-1\), would give
\[
s(x)\le9(k-1)<9k,
\]
a contradiction.

We now apply these observations to the reachable set at the special index
\[
n_k=10^k-1.
\]
Fix \(k\ge1\), and take any \(v\in R_{n_k}\). At the preceding stage there is some \(u\in R_{n_k-1}\) such that, at the final step, \(v\) is one of the two values
\[
v=n_ku
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
v=Z(n_ku).                                                       \tag{14}
\]
As proved above, every reachable value is positive, so \(u>0\). Hence
\[
M=n_ku=(10^k-1)u
\]
is a positive multiple of \(10^k-1\). By the lemma,
\[
s(M)\ge9k.                                                      \tag{15}
\]
If the product was retained in (14), then \(v=M\), and (15) gives \(s(v)\ge9k\). If zero deletion was chosen, then \(v=Z(M)\), and the digit-sum invariance (1) gives
\[
s(v)=s(Z(M))=s(M)\ge9k.
\]
Thus in either of the two possible cases at the final step,
\[
s(v)\ge9k.
\]
Applying (13), we find that every reachable value at index \(10^k-1\) obeys
\[
v\ge10^{k-1}.
\]
Since \(a(10^k-1)\) is the minimum of all these reachable values, it too satisfies
\[
a(10^k-1)\ge10^{k-1},
\]
which is the promised lower bound.

Finally, suppose for contradiction that the conjectured bound existed: assume that there were a natural number \(B\) such that
\[
a(n)\le B
\]
for every natural number \(n\). Choose \(k=B+1\). The lower bound just proved gives
\[
a(10^{B+1}-1)\ge10^{(B+1)-1}=10^B,
\]
whereas the assumed global bound gives
\[
a(10^{B+1}-1)\le B.
\]
But \(10^B>B\) for every natural number \(B\) (for \(B=0\) this is \(1>0\), and the general statement also follows immediately by induction). Hence these two inequalities are incompatible.

Therefore no natural number \(B\) can satisfy \(a(n)\le B\) for every \(n\). The sequence A374265 is unbounded, so the boundedness conjecture is false.
